messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric harvester (sinusoidal current source $I_p$, capacitance $C_p$, leakage $R_{leak}$).
    *   Output requirements:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Piezo characteristics: $I_p$ varies (30-100 $\mu$A), $f$ varies (80-100 Hz), $C_p$ varies (25-30 nF).
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2 \pi f C_p)$. For S1: $50\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100\text{Hz} \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{ V}$.
    *   Load $R_L$ varies (150 k$\Omega$ to 2200 k$\Omega$).

    *   Full-bridge rectifier (FBR) failed on:
        *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{ V} < 1.8\text{ V}$ (Voltage drop too high, too much current drawn).
        *   S3 (strong excitation, light load): $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V} > 3.6\text{ V}$ (Overvoltage).
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{ V} < 1.8\text{ V}$ (Voltage drop too high relative to $V_{oc}$).
        *   S5 (low freq): $dV$ failed (possibly not settled).

    *   *Challenge 1: Voltage boost.* To overcome diode drops and increase $V_{avg}$ for S2 and S4, we need more than a passive rectifier. An SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or a SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) circuit is typically used to flip the voltage across $C_p$.
    *   *Challenge 2: Overvoltage protection.* S3 shows we need a clamp (Zener) to keep $V_{out} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   *Challenge 3: Ripple/Stability.* A large storage capacitor $C_{out}$ is needed to minimize $V_{pp}$ and $dV$.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI-like (with Full Bridge and Inductor Flip).**
        *   Standard SSHI flips the voltage at the peaks using an inductor and a switch. This significantly increases the extracted power and output voltage.
        *   Structure: FBR + Inductor + Switch + SYNC.
        *   The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are placed to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks.
        *   Wait, the simplest "quasi-SSHI" involves an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo, or an inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in series with a rectifier.
        *   Actually, a simpler approach for power enhancement is the "Parallel-SSHI" or "Series-SSHI". Let's try a basic inductor-switch inverter across the piezo terminals.
        *   Wait, if I put $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo, they only affect $C_p$ if they are activated at the peaks.
        *   Better: a standard SSHI circuit. But we have limited components (16).
        *   Let's try: FBR $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$ $\rightarrow$ Zener. To improve $V_{avg}$, we can use an active inverter.
        *   Alternatively, a "Buck" or "Boost" structure, but SYNC is limited to switching at peaks.

    *   **Design 2: SECE-like (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).**
        *   SECE uses an inductor and a switch to transfer all the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ at the peak.
        *   Topology: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Switch $\rightarrow$ Inductor $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        *   This is generally more efficient than FBR for low $V_{oc}$.

    *   **Design 3: Improved FBR with Zener and higher storage.**
        *   The FBR failed on S2, S3, S4. S3 is an overvoltage issue (easy fix: Zener). S2 and S4 are undervoltage issues.
        *   To fix S2/S4, we must reduce the voltage drop or increase the voltage gain.
        *   A charge pump or a switch-capacitor circuit? No, the SYNC controller is designed for $L-C_p$ inversion.
        *   Let's focus on the $L-C_p$ inverter.

    *   The SYNC controller closes the switch for $t_{on}$ at the piezo voltage extrema.
    *   If we place $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo (pzp, pzn), at the peak, the switch closes, and the energy in $C_p$ oscillates into $L$, then back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity. This "flips" the voltage, effectively increasing the voltage swing across the rectifier.
    *   Circuit:
        1.  FBR (4 x DSCH) from (pzp, pzn) to (out, 0).
        2.  $C_{out}$ from (out, 0).
        3.  $D_{zener}$ (DZ33) from (0, out) to clamp $V_{out}$ at 3.3V.
        4.  $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo: $L$ between pzp and n1, $S$ between n1 and pzn.
        5.  SYNC $G1$ controls $S$. $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$. $C_p=25\text{nF}$, so if $L=10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.

    *   Wait, the standard SSHI inversion is often done *before* the rectifier.
    *   Connectivity:
        *   $D1$: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
        *   $D2$: pzn $\rightarrow$ out
        *   $D3$: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp
        *   $D4$: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn
        *   $C_{out}$: out $\rightarrow$ 0
        *   $DZ$: 0 $\rightarrow$ out
        *   $L1$: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
        *   $S1$: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn (ctrl: G1)
        *   $G1$: ton=..., edges="both", phase=0.0.

    *   Actually, if the switch is in parallel with the piezo, it will just short the piezo. We need the inductor to create the resonant flip.
    *   Correct SSHI (Parallel): $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo. When $S$ closes, $C_p$ and $L$ form a resonant circuit. $V_{pzp}$ flips from $+V$ to $-V$. This increases the voltage across the rectifier.

    *   Wait, if $S$ closes at the peak, the current from $C_p$ flows through $L$. The voltage $V_{pzp}$ starts at $V_{peak}$ and goes to $-V_{peak}$ in $t = \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   Does this work with a Full Bridge? Yes. The bridge extracts the energy. The flip helps "push" more charge into the storage capacitor by preventing the voltage from spending too much time near the diode drop thresholds.

    *   $C_p \approx 25\text{nF}$.
    *   $L \approx 1\text{mH}$ to $10\text{mH}$.
    *   $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
    *   $C_{out}$ needs to be large enough to keep ripple low. $2.2\mu\text{F}$ was used in FBR, let's try $10\mu\text{F}$.
    *   $DZ33$ (Zener) for S3.

    *   The "Parallel-SSHI" can be problematic because the inductor might ring or the switch might be too slow (though these switches are ideal).
    *   Alternative: "Series-SSHI". The inductor is in series with the rectifier.
    *   Wait, another simple and effective topology is the "Half-Bridge" or "Single-Ended" if the piezo is floating, but the model specifies pzp and pzn.
    *   Let's try the Parallel-SSHI (Inductor-Switch in parallel) as it's a known power booster.

    *   S1: Nominal. SSHI should increase $V_{avg}$.
    *   S2: Heavy load. Higher power from SSHI should keep $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   S3: Strong excitation. Zener DZ33 will clamp $V_{out} \le 3.3\text{ V} + \text{ripple}$.
    *   S4: Weak excitation. Higher efficiency of SSHI should help.
    *   S5: Low freq. Should be fine.
    *   S6: Hot/Cp change. Should be fine.

    *   FBR: 4 diodes
    *   Zener: 1 diode
    *   Storage: 1 capacitor
    *   Inverter: 1 inductor, 1 switch, 1 SYNC
    *   Total: 8 components. (Well within the 16 limit).

    *   *Proposal 1 (SSHI-FBR):* FBR + Parallel L-S Inverter + Zener Clamp.
    *   *Proposal 2 (SECE-like):* This usually involves a switch that connects the piezo to the storage cap through an inductor. Let's try a simplified version:
        *   $S1$ connects pzp $\rightarrow$ n1.
        *   $L1$ connects n1 $\rightarrow$ out.
        *   $D1$ connects out $\rightarrow$ pzp (blocking).
        *   Wait, SECE is more complex. Let's stick to SSHI and maybe a modified FBR.
    *   *Proposal 3 (Charge Pump / Voltage Doubler):* If $V_{oc}$ is too low, a Dickson charge pump could work, but they are less efficient and require a clock. SYNC is our only clock.
    *   Actually, let's try two variations of the SSHI. One with a full bridge, and one with a half-bridge if we can find a way to bias the piezo.
    *   But the piezo is a current source in parallel with $C_p$, and it's between pzp and pzn. A full bridge is the most robust.

    *   If $S$ is in parallel with the piezo (pzp-n1, n1-pzn), it creates a loop: $C_p \rightarrow L \rightarrow S$. This flips the voltage on $C_p$.
    *   Wait, if the rectifier is also connected to pzp and pzn, does the flip still work?
    *   Yes, because the rectifier diodes are only conducting when $|V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}| > 2 \cdot V_{diode}$. During the short $t_{on}$ (microseconds), the inductor current dominates.

    *   $L \approx 4.7\text{mH}$
    *   $C_{out} \approx 10\mu\text{F}$
    *   $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{4.7\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 10.8\mu\text{s}$.

    *   Actually, to be safe, let's provide a few topology options.
    *   Option 1: Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    *   Option 2: Parallel SSHI + FBR (No Zener, but maybe the optimizer can find a value? No, S3 needs a clamp).
    *   Wait, let's try Option 2 as a "Standard SSHI" with a different switch placement.
    *   Instead of Parallel SSHI, let's try "Series SSHI". In Series SSHI, the inductor is in series with the rectifier. However, Parallel is more common for current sources.

    *   Let's refine the Parallel SSHI.
        *   $D1: \text{pzp} \rightarrow \text{out}$
        *   $D2: \text{pzn} \rightarrow \text{out}$
        *   $D3: 0 \rightarrow \text{pzp}$
        *   $D4: 0 \rightarrow \text{pzn}$
        *   $C1: \text{out} \rightarrow 0$
        *   $DZ1: 0 \rightarrow \text{out}$
        *   $L1: \text{pzp} \rightarrow \text{n1}$
        *   $S1: \text{n1} \rightarrow \text{pzn}$, ctrl: $G1$
        *   $G1: \text{ton}=1\text{e-5}, \text{edges}=\text{"both"}, \text{phase}=0$

    *   Wait, one more thing: the reference design failed S2 and S4 because $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{ V}$. These are cases where the power extracted is just barely not enough. SSHI should definitely help.

    *   Is there any other way to get more voltage?
    *   A "Voltage Doubler" (Greinacher circuit):
        *   $C1$ in series with piezo.
        *   $D1, D2, C2, C3$.
        *   This might be too complex with the current source model.
    *   Let's stick with SSHI.

    *   One last check on the Zener: $DZ33$ has a breakdown of $3.3\text{ V}$. With ripple, it might hit $3.6\text{ V}$. That's acceptable.

    *   *Self-Correction on SSHI:* For a current source, the "flip" occurs at the peaks of the *voltage*. The SYNC controller triggers at the extrema of the piezo voltage (which are the zero crossings of the piezo current). This is exactly what we need.

    *   *Proposed Design 1: "SSHIFBR"*
        *   Components: D1-D4 (FBR), C1 (out), DZ1 (Zener), L1, S1, G1.
    *   *Proposed Design 2: "SSHIFBR_L"*
        *   Same as SSHIFBR but with a different L/C arrangement? No, the optimizer handles values. Let's change the connectivity.
        *   What if we use a half-bridge? (Piezo is floating).
        *   Piezo pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ out, pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ 0. (This is just a half-wave rectifier).
        *   Wait, the piezo model is a current source $I_p$ in parallel with $C_p$ between pzp and pzn.
        *   A half-wave rectifier: pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ out, pzn $\rightarrow$ 0. This doesn't work because the current $I_p$ must return.
        *   So FBR is best.

    *   *Proposed Design 3: "SECE_Simple"*
        *   SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) is often: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Switch $\rightarrow$ Inductor $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        *   $S1$: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1 (ctrl: G1)
        *   $L1$: n1 $\rightarrow$ out
        *   $D1$: out $\rightarrow$ pzp (wait, no)
        *   Let's try: $S1$ connects the piezo to the storage cap via an inductor at the peak.
        *   $S1$: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1 (ctrl: G1)
        *   $L1$: n1 $\rightarrow$ out
        *   $D1$: out $\rightarrow$ n1 (no)
        *   Let's stick to the SSHI-FBR. It's the most reliable booster for this kind of setup.

    *   *Refining SSHI-FBR one more time:*
        *   FBR:
            *   D1: pzp, out
            *   D2: pzn, out
            *   D3: 0, pzp
            *   D4: 0, pzn
        *   Storage/Clamp:
            *   C1: out, 0
            *   DZ1: 0, out
        *   Inverter:
            *   L1: pzp, n1
            *   S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
            *   G1: ton=1e-5, edges=both, phase=0.0

    *   Wait, let's consider the "Phase". In SSHI, we want to flip the voltage exactly at the peak. The SYNC controller says "closes its switches... at the piezo voltage extrema". This is exactly the peak. Phase=0.0 is correct.

    *   Wait, let's check the $C_p$ value again. $C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
        $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. If $L=10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = 15.7\mu\text{s}$. If $L=1\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = 5\mu\text{s}$.
        The range for `ton` is 1e-7 to 0.001. $15\mu\text{s}$ is well within.

    *   Final check on connectivity:
        D1: [pzp, out]
        D2: [pzn, out]
        D3: [0, pzp]
        D4: [0, pzn]
        C1: [out, 0]
        DZ1: [0, out]
        L1: [pzp, n1]
        S1: [n1, pzn]
        G1: SYNC

    *   One detail: The reference design used $C_{out} = 2.2\mu\text{F}$. For ripple $\le 50\text{mV}$, we might need more. Let's suggest $10\mu\text{F}$ to start, though the optimizer will refine it.

    *   Wait, the reference design failed S2 and S4. S4 is the hardest (weak excitation $30\mu\text{A}$).
        $V_{oc} = 30\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 1.91\text{ V}$.
        With a full bridge of DSCH ($\approx 0.25\text{V}$ drop per diode, so $0.5\text{V}$ total), $V_{out} \approx 1.91 - 0.5 = 1.41\text{ V}$.
        This explains why the FBR failed ($V_{avg} = 1.51\text{ V}$).
        SSHI increases the effective voltage by flipping $C_p$, allowing the rectifier to see a higher voltage.

    *   One more topology to try: what if we use a "Synchronous Rectifier" instead of a diode bridge?
        We have only 4 switches. A full bridge needs 4 switches.
        S1: pzp, out
        S2: pzn, out
        S3: 0, pzp
        S4: 0, pzn
        But we need a controller for each. We only have 2 SYNCs.
        So we can't do a full synchronous rectifier.

    *   What about a half-bridge synchronous rectifier?
        We could use one SYNC to toggle two switches. But the SYNC controller is defined as "closes *its* switches", implying one SYNC can control multiple switches if they share the same `ctrl` ID.
        Let's check: "S switch... 'ctrl': id of a SYNC". Yes, multiple switches can have the same `ctrl`.
        So we could have:
        S1: pzp, out (ctrl: G1)
        S2: 0, pzn (ctrl: G1)
        And G1 triggers at the positive peak.
        S3: pzn, out (ctrl: G2)
        S4: 0, pzp (ctrl: G2)
        And G2 triggers at the negative peak.
        This would eliminate the diode drops!
        However, this is just a synchronous rectifier, not a power booster like SSHI. SSHI is generally more powerful because it actively flips the charge.

    *   Let's go with SSHI-FBR. It's the most likely to solve both the undervoltage (S2, S4) and overvoltage (S3) problems.

    *   *Refining SSHI-FBR components:*
        D1 [pzp, out] DSCH
        D2 [pzn, out] DSCH
        D3 [0, pzp] DSCH
        D4 [0, pzn] DSCH
        DZ1 [0, out] DZ33
        C1 [out, 0] 10uF
        L1 [pzp, n1] 4.7mH
        S1 [n1, pzn] (ctrl: G1)
        G1 [ton=1e-5, edges=both, phase=0]

    *   Wait, I can propose up to 3. Let's propose:
        1.  SSHIFBR: (The one above).
        2.  SSHIFBR_half: A version with a half-bridge (just in case) - No, let's try something else.
        3.  SSHIFBR_C: (Same connectivity, different labels? No, that's not a different structure).
        How about an "Inductor-based Boost" (SECE)?
        SECE Connectivity:
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl: G1)
        L1: n1, out
        D1: out, n1 (no, that's not right)
        Actually, let's try a "Voltage Doubler" with the SYNC.
        S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl: G1)
        C1: n1, 0
        D1: n1, out
        C2: out, 0
        This is getting complex. Let's stick to SSHI-FBR and maybe a variation.
        Variation: Instead of a full bridge, what if we use a half-bridge with a capacitor for bias?
        C_bias: pzp, pzn
        Actually, FBR is the safest.

        Let's try:
        Design 1: SSHI-FBR (as described).
        Design 2: SSHI-FBR with a capacitor in series with the inductor to make it a resonant tank? No.
        Design 3: SSHI-FBR but with only 2 diodes and a capacitor (Half-bridge).
        $D1$: pzp, out
        $D2$: pzn, out
